tossups.text: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is the failure of this structure caused by haemorrhagic bacterial infection. The neural crest derived cells of this structure are directly innervated by preganglionic sympathetic neurons and the arteries supplying this structure are the only ones in the splanchnic bed to dilate during stress. The cortex of this organ has a fetal zone that regresses in neonatal life and its zona fasciculata produces cortisol in the adult. For 10 points, name these paired endocrine organs that release catecholamines and sit atop the kidneys.

In the X.509 protocol, this concept is encoded by the DN value, which is also used in LDAP. Software made by Okta specializes in the "management" of this concept. This concept can be established with the help of timestamped tickets by the Kerberos protocol. "Providers" of this concept grant users access across multiple applications in SSO schemes. This concept is encoded by the radiofrequency signal of a RF chip and the integrated circuit chip in a "smart card." "What you have" is one of three "factors" used to verify this concept in MFA, which can also incorporate biometric data. About 10% of Americans are victims of the "theft" of, for 10 points, what concept often verified using documents like a driver's license or passport?
acceptableAnswers: prompt on verification by asking “of what?”
prompt on descriptive answers that refer to who

tossups.text: A cherub in a painting from this country places his finger to his lips to "shush" two Venus putti from giving away an affair. In a painting from this country, a reclined lover hiding in the bushes was modeled after the painting's patron, the Baron de Saint-Julien. In a painting from this country, a woman in a pink dress rides on a red leather seat that is pushed by her unknowing husband. For 10 points, name this home country of the Rococo artist Jean-Honore Fragonard ["jeen aa-naw-ray fra-guh-nrd"].

He wrote about a man named Chapter 11 who bankrupts Hercules's Hot Dogs in a novel in which the protagonist learns from his grandmother Desdemona that Lefty was his brother. That character shortens his name due to his 5-alpha reductase deficiency. This man collected a bunch of other author's love stories and wrote an introduction for them in a collection that quotes Catullus in his My Mistress's Sparrow is Dead. In the other novel by this man, the Lisbons lose all five of their children: Cecilia, Lux, Bonnie, Mary, and Therese. For 10 points, name this contemporary American author The Virgin Suicides that wrote about a woman named Calliope who shortens her name to Cal in Middlesex.

The ambiguous usage of this word in poems by W. H. Auden and others is the subject of a Bonnie Costello book which also discusses the recent resurgence in the use of this word in poetry. This is the second word in the two-word poem that was delivered during a 1975 Harvard commencement address by Muhammad Ali. A poem starting with this word asks "Why should the world be over-wise, in counting all our tears and sighs?" That poem starting with this word describes an object that "grins and lies" and "hides our cheeks and shades our eyes." In a poem from the collection The Bean Eaters, this word appears at the end of seven of the eight lines, despite being the first word in all of the poem's three-word sentences. For 10 points, name this pronoun which appears before phrases like "jazz June" and "real cool" in a Gwendolyn Brooks poem.

This type of composition names a 1932 piece that uses elements from the Ignacio Piñeiro song "Échale Salsita" and was inspired by a trip to a Caribbean island. The second part of J.S. Bach's Clavier-Übung includes the Italian Concerto and a French one of these works. Mendelssohn's Scottish Symphony was composed around the same time as one of these works that depicts rolling waves. Shostakovich composed a "Festive" one of these works and Brahms composed a "Tragic" one. This type of composition is often played at the beginning of an opera. For 10 points, name these compositions, one of which by Tchaikovsky was named for the year 1812.

After a sailor tries to kiss this character and calls her a "witch-baby," this character declares "my father is the Prince of the Air" and threatens to send a storm after his ship. This character is described as a "half-fledged angel of judgment" after scaring off a group of children throwing mud at her. This character tells Mr. Wilson that she was "plucked...off the bush of wild roses that grew by the prison-door" after being asked who made her. Throughout the novel this character appears in, she repeatedly asks why a minister keeps his hand over his heart. This character asks her father if he will "take my hand, and mother's hand" at noon as they stand on a scaffold and watch a meteor fall. For 10 points, name this daughter of Arthur Dimmesdale and Hester Prynne.

This thinker cited the lack of religious "mystery" during the scholastic era as part of an argument by elimination against prejudiced definitions of religion. That book by this thinker compared religious symbols named for an Ojibwe word that represent "god and of the society" to modern national flags. Marcel Mauss added the word "total" to a term coined by this thinker, who analyzed totemism in The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life. Robert Merton adapted this thinker's ideas when creating strain theory. This thinker argued that deviance was necessary to clarify norms in a book that found higher rates of one act in Protestants than Catholics. For 10 points, name this foundational French sociologist who wrote about anomie in the monograph Suicide.

In this state, Barnett Walensky was convicted of negligent homicide after 492 people died in a fire at the Cocoanut Grove nightclub. A distillery holding tank in this state's largest city burst in 1919, causing a flood of molasses that killed 21 people. A trial presided over by Webster Thayer in this state centering around a shoe factory robbery led to the execution of two anarchist Italian-American immigrants. Sacco and Vanzetti were executed in this state, which is also where Whitey Bulger's gang operated in its largest city's "Southie" neighborhood. For 10 points, name this most populous state in New England.

This musician once added the lyrics "Oh, memory" before an instrumental break in a rendition of the Hoagy Carmichael song "Stardust". This musician was originally a member of the Creole band in Chicago along with his mentor Joe King Oliver. He created an album with songs from Porgy and Bess which he collaborated on with Ella Fitzgerald. Many recordings by this musician were with his Hot Five and Hot Seven bands, and this man was the first person to record a song that begins "I see trees of green, red roses too." For 10 points, name this innovative jazz trumpeter nicknamed "Satchmo" who raspily sang songs like "What a Wonderful World."

Carl Troll has argued that this empire's rise was linked to the sub-freezing temperatures that allowed for production of their staple crop, a potato product called chuño. This empire's leader was believed to be a son of the god Inti, and this empire kept records using quipu [kee-poo], or knotted strings. This empire's language was Quechua, and these people built Machu Picchu. This empire was conquered by Francisco Pizarro. For 10 points, name this empire of the Andes Mountains which had its capital at Cuzco in Peru.

Mos1 is one of these that belong to the Mariner/TC1 family, and an example produced in-vitro is called the "Sleeping Beauty" system. The Tn family forms composite structures of these entities, while one widespread example leads to hybrid dysgenesis in fruitflies, that being the P element. Their ends often possess inverted repeats, and, in a similar fashion to certain viruses, one type uses a reverse transcript to "copy and paste" DNA, known as the retro type. For 10 points, identify these entities discovered in maize by Barbara McClintock, that are also called jumping genes.

The narrator of this book states that the most popular character is an undertaker who hits a dog for causing a commotion. That event occurs at a funeral for Peter Wilks, whose savings are stolen by two characters claiming to come from England and France. In this book, Harney and Miss Sophia elope during a conflict between the Grangerfords and Shepherdsons. Before meeting the aforementioned Duke and Dauphin, the main characters are dismayed when a bout of fog causes them to pass Cairo and miss the entry to the Ohio River. For 10 points, name this novel about the runaway slave Jim and a comrade of Tom Sawyer sailing down the Mississippi, a book by Mark Twain.

The "forgotten alternatives" presented by 19th-century history are discussed in a C. Vann Woodward book titled for the "strange career" of this figure. A book titled for this figure examines the HUD's "One Strike" policy in a chapter on "The Cruel Hand." This figure was introduced by Thomas D. Rice, who wrote a piece in which he exclaims "wheel about, and turn about, and do just so." The "undercaste" created by the War on Drugs and mass incarceration is discussed in a Michelle Alexander book titled for the "new" this figure. This figure, who titles a minstrel song titled "Jump [him]," is the namesake of a legal regime that revived the 1865 Black Codes and was targeted by the Brown v. Board of Education decision. For 10 points, Southern racial segregation laws were nicknamed for what fictional man?

this structure is essential for hepatic portal system. It plays a key role in the digestive system and is one of the most studied parts of human anatomy. For ten points, name this liver-related structure.
tossups.explanation: The liver is a key component of the Digestive system, involved in hepatic portal system.

tossups.text: In a philosophical dialogue from this modern-day country, the king of the Khazars is shown that human flourishing consists in union with the tenth and lowest divine intellect. That work is the Kuzari by Judah Halevi. A school from this nation included the author of Metaphysical Disputations and a just war theorist who condemned his nation's actions in the Americas. An existentialist from this country discusses "men of flesh and bone" burdened with awareness of their mortality in The Tragic Sense of Life. Another philosopher from this county declared "I am myself and my circumstances" and denounced the "mass-man" in The Revolt of the Masses. For 10 points, name this modern-day country once home to José Ortega y Gasset, Miguel de Unamuno, and the School of Salamanca.

This architect designed the interior of the Monsoon Restaurant in Sapporo, Japan and created the Bergisel Ski Jump in Innsbruck. Other works include a nautilus-shaped tent erected in Central Park to house artwork inspired by the 2.55 handbag, the Chanel Mobile Art Pavilion, and the proposed design for the Cardiff Bay Opera House. Another project interchanges walls and floors "like a ribbon in space" - that museum, the MAXXI in Rome, contrasts with Cincinnati's Contemporary Arts Center, built as a series of cubes and prisms held together by stilts. This designer of the Guangzhou Opera House. and student of Rem Koolhaas, is best known for a building organized in a scissor-like manner to "connect [the] ground floor and first floor into a continuous field," - that project in Liepzig is the BMW Central Building. For 10 points, name this deconstructivist architect who was born in Iraq and studied in Britain, the first female recipient of the Pritzker Prize.

Block codes are often described using one of these structures over GF1.. A prominent example of a contravariant functor is the duality on the category of these structures. A generalization of these structures is defined over a ring and is a module. A subset of these structures is the subject of the Steinitz exchange lemma. Over a field F, they can be defined as an abelian group, A, and a ring homomorphism from F to the endomorphism ring of A, which maps the identity to the identity. One property of these structures can be found by adding the dimension of the image and kernel of a linear transformation according to the rank-nullity theorem. These structures are closed under addition and scalar multiplication. For 10 points, identify these spaces studied in linear algebra.

A boiled form of this dish is the Acadian Poutine Râpée, which is eaten with fruit, sugar, or maple syrup. A steamed version of this food popular in Tibet and Nepal is called momo. Hyacinth of Poland is the patron saint of one type of this food, which is produced in America by the brand Mrs. T's. One type of this food filled with gelatinous soup comes from Shanghai and is called xiaolongbao ("shyao-long-baow"). It's not pasta, but gnocchi ("nyo-kee") is a type of this dish. Jiaozi ("jow-zee") differs from a form of this food often served in soups, wontons, by the shape of the wrapper used. For 10 points, pierogies and potstickers are versions of what food made of a filling wrapped by a starchy dough?

In this man's third novel, he expounded on the theory of AB plus CD yields AD plus BC and applied laws of chemistry to human relationships; that novel was titled Elective Affinities. In another one of his works, Gretchen is saved by God while her lover, the titular character, made a deal with Mephistopheles, and in another work, the title character's love for Lotte, who marries Albert, turns into tragedy as he commits suicide in the end. For 10 points, identify this German author of Faust and The Sorrows of Young Werther.

parts.text: Name this method in which a protein of interest is engineered by making many copies of its gene, applying mutagenesis, then performing a screening assay to measure their function and isolating the highest-performing proteins. The cycle is repeated, causing a situation analogous to climbing a hill on a fitness landscape.
The first two steps of a directed evolution cycle can be combined into one by using a "mutagenic" variant of this technique, which can use "high-fidelity" proteins like Pfu.

A very simple example of a screening assay in molecular biology is this one, in which the gene of interest is cloned into a site in the middle of the lacZ gene inside a bacterium. The cells are then plated on X-gal to visually-distinguish successful recombinants.

bonuses.leadin: This method is useful compared to strict rational approaches because there are 20 raised to the N proteins with N amino acids-too many to individually synthesize and test. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this region right under the earth's crust.
The Moho discontinuity is right above this region, which is bounded on the bottom by the Gutenberg Discontinuity.
The Moho Discontinuity was detected by the increase in speed of this type of body wave, which are longitudinal and can travel through air as sound

bonuses.leadin: It was discovered by its namesake when he observed that certain seismic waves increase speed at this point. For 10 points each:

parts.text: This piece symbolizes the flow and scenery of the titular river; it is adapted from the Italian Renaissance song Fuggi, fuggi, fuggi da questo cielo.
The Moldau is the second movement of this patriotically-named symphonic poem with six movements that symbolizes various attributes about Bohemia.
Smetana also composed this opera about how Marenka defies the arranged marriage that her parents set up for her and marries her lover Jenik instead.

bonuses.leadin: Identify some works by the Czech composer, Bedrich Smetana, for 10 points each.

parts.text: Name this 2010 novel whose title state of being is arguably achieved by its character Patty Berglund when she is kicked out of her Georgetown house by her husband, Walter.
Freedom is a novel by this contemporary author who wrote about the Lambert family in The Corrections.

While attending the University of Virginia, Patty Berglund's son Joey reconsiders his worldview after this event. In his poem "Somebody Blew Up America," Amiri Baraka asks why "4000 Israeli workers" stayed home during this event.

bonuses.leadin: While traveling to Argentina with Jenna, one character in this novel searches through his feces for his wedding ring, which he had accidentally swallowed. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this author who wrote about a life-sapping substance in "The Colour Out of Space." This author wrote about "Great Old Ones" such as Hastur in his Cthulhu Mythos.

Lovecraft is best known for his work in this subgenre of speculative fiction, which he described as "more than secret murder, bloody bones." A Lovecraft essay contains "Notes on Writing" in this genre, whose "new" form is associated with Jeff VanderMeer.
This author brought what would later be called New Weird fiction into the mainstream with a novel set in New Crobuzon. He also wrote the novella The Last Days of New Paris.

bonuses.leadin: A meteorite lands in the New England town of Arkham in a short story by this author. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this controversial painting that features a black cat. The confrontational gaze and posture of this painting's subject were inspired by Titian's Venus of Urbino.
Olympia is a work by this Impressionist painter, who included a large mirror behind a barmaid in A Bar at the Folies-Bergère.
This other artist was the model for the nude in Olympia. Her own works include a self-portrait that was accepted for the 1876 Salon, at which Manet's own self-portrait was rejected.

bonuses.leadin: Lorraine O'Grady wrote that "to name ourselves rather than be named we must first see ourselves" in an essay that analyzes this painting's Eurocentric depiction of a maid. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this 1951 novel in which Marco Polo claims to be "saying something about Venice" each time he describes one of the title metropolises to Kublai Khan.
Invisible Cities was written by this Italian author of the science-inspired short story collections t zero and Cosmicomics and the metafictional novel If on a winter's night a traveler.

In 1968, Raymond Queneau invited Calvino to join this literary group, whose name is short for a French phrase meaning "workshop of potential literature". It advocated constrained writing and counted François Le Lionnais and George Perec among its other members.

bonuses.leadin: Berenice, the last of this book's title entities, is alternately just and unjust, while Ersilia contains no people but merely strings charting the former inhabitants' relationships. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Identify this constitutional clause, which is found in two amendments. This clause prevents people from being deprived of life, liberty, or property.
The due process clause can be found in the fifth amendment and in this other amendment, which applies the due process clause to states. This amendment made all people born in the U.S. citizens.

In Bolling v. Sharpe, part of Brown v. Board, this doctrine was established when the court applied the equal protection clause of the fourteenth amendment through the due process clause of the fifth amendment.

bonuses.leadin: This clause is applied procedurally, substantively, and as a protection against vague laws. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this Mesoamerican sport, the goal of which was to hit its namesake rubber objects through wall-mounted rings using only the hips.
The largest ball court ruins are found in this pre-Columbian Mayan city, whose main attraction is the Temple to Kukulkan, a massive stepped pyramid nicknamed "El Caudillo."

According to the Codex Mendoza, the ball game was also played by the Aztecs. The Codex Mendoza was written to help Charles V, a member of this royal family that ruled Austria, to understand Aztec history.

bonuses.leadin: This activity was performed on courts at places like Uaxactun ["uw-ah-zac-tan"] and other Mayan cities in the Peten basin. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Abbot Suger kick-started the Gothic style with his plans for this cathedral where French kings were traditionally buried.
This cathedral fifty miles outside of Paris has a labyrinth on its floor. Its stained glass includes the Blue Virgin Window, and it was the first building to require flying buttresses.
Napoleon was crowned at this famed cathedral in Paris whose south tower holds the bell Emmanuel. Its Galerie des Chimères is named for its many Gothic-style gargoyles.

bonuses.leadin: For 10 points each, name these Gothic cathedrals.

parts.text: The Supreme Court upheld this overhaul of healthcare that was signed into law in 2010.
The ACA's individual mandate was ruled constitutional due to Congress' power to do this rather than spend revenues.
This Chief Justice wrote the assenting opinion and was likely the swing vote in the 5-4 decision.

bonuses.leadin: National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius was a recent landmark court case. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Bromothymol Blue is one of these compounds used in acid-base chemistry to visually represent the pH of a solution. These compounds change color at particular pH values.
This ferromagnetic element with atomic number 27 is often used in blue pigments and forms a namesake blue glass. Its 60-isotope is used medically for radiation therapy.
The pigment Prussian Blue is a complex compound of iron and this anion. It attacks an iminium ion to form an aminonitrile in the Strecker amino acid synthesis.

bonuses.leadin: Answer some questions about things that are blue in chemistry. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this author who detailed the deaths of the Clutter family in Holcomb, Kansas in a 1966 non-fiction novel that pioneered the genre of true crime.
This Truman Capote novel set in Skully's Landing is about 13-year-old Joel Knox, whose father is completely paralyzed and communicates by dropping red tennis balls down the stairs.

Other Voices, Other Rooms is a novel in the "Southern" variant of this literary genre. This genre of Stoker's Dracula emphasizes themes of strong emotion and terror and gets its name from a style of architecture.

bonuses.leadin: A novel by this author recounts how Floyd Wells tipped Dick Hickock and Perry Smith off about a family safe, leading to the central murders. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this president who ordered the dropping of two atomic bombs on Japan. He succeeded to the presidency after the death of Franklin D. Roosevelt.
In 1948, Truman won an election to become president in his own right. He narrowly defeated this New York Republican, despite early media projections that this man would win.
After the 1948 election, a famous photo shows a triumphant Truman holding up a newspaper from this city with the erroneous headline "DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN."

bonuses.leadin: This man made many speeches attacking the "Do Nothing Congress." For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name the primary structure associated with sympathetic vs parasympathetic.
What is the main function of the cranial nerve in the nervous system?
Name another component of the nervous system related to sympathetic vs parasympathetic.

bonuses.leadin: For 10 points each, answer these questions about the human nervous system.

parts.text: The spiritual leader of a shtetl was one of these men, whose name means "master" in Hebrew. These leaders are ordained during semikhah after studying the Talmud.

In addition to rabbis, most shtetls had a shokhet or ritual slaughterer, who made sure meat was prepared according to this set of Jewish dietary laws. Food that meets the standards of these laws is deemed kosher.

Shtetls in Poland and Lithuania were governed by these community political bodies usually consisting of at least eight men. Members of these bodies met up to form the more centralized Council of Four Lands.

bonuses.leadin: Answer the following about social roles that you would expect to find in an 18th-century Eastern European shtetl, for 10 points each:

parts.text: This composer of La Clementina and some notable string quartets also wrote a cello concerto in B flat major that was extensively altered by Friedrich Grützmacher.
Best known for an 1890 opera that features such characters as Santuzza, Lola, and Turiddu, this man also composed such works as Guglielmo Ratcliff and L'Amico Fritz.

Thanks to his prolific use of the technique in his many harpsichord sonatas, a certain type of arpeggiated chord accompaniment is known as this man's "bass." This student of Antonio Lotti also composed operas for voice and harpsichord.

bonuses.leadin: For 10 points each, name these Italian composers.

parts.text: Name this theorem.
Wiles' proof relied heavily on these mathematical objects, which over the real numbers can be defined as an equation of the form y2=x3+ax+b.

In order to prove Fermat's Last Theorem, Wiles proved this conjecture for semi-stable curves. It states that, for every elliptic curve, there is a modular form with the same Dirichlet L-series. This conjecture is now also known as the Modularity Theorem.

bonuses.leadin: This theorem, which states that no three positive integers A, B, and C can satisfy An+Bn=Cn for integral values of n greater than 2, was finally proven by Andrew Wiles. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this type of place. Another Danish example of this type of place is Tivoli Gardens, which contains a notable wooden attraction called the Rutschebanen ("root-shu-baynen").
Bakken and Tivoli Gardens are both located within this city, the capital of Denmark.
This amusement park is Denmark's largest tourist attraction outside of Copenhagen. A 2023 attraction at this amusement park is themed around designing and testing Ferraris.

bonuses.leadin: Since it opened in 1583, Denmark's Dyrehavsbakken ("deer-avs-bakken") is the world's oldest operating one of these places. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this Shakespearean play subtitled the Moor of Venice.
This other play by Shakespeare is set in Padua and centers on Petruchio's courtship of Katherine, the title figure.
Tamora, Queen of the Goths, eats her two sons as baked meats in this Shakespearean tragedy about the title Roman general.

bonuses.leadin: The title character of this play has a stormy marriage to Desdemona and is tricked by Iago. For 10 points each:
